# Smart Pointers

## :dart: Learning goals of this lecture
- Smart pointers to reduce dangling storage.

## Smart pointers

In C++11 smart pointers where introduced, the idea is to have a wrapper class that manages the lifetime of the object it points to.
They were introduced to help ensure that programs are free of memory and resource leaks and are exception-safe.

![Source <https://xkcd.com/371>](https://imgs.xkcd.com/comics/compiler_complaint.png){.lightbox}

(and to keep your compiler happy)

## Smart pointers - Reasons

There are several problems with pointers that smart pointers try to solve or at least mitigate

- Memory Leaks: This occurs when memory is repeatedly allocated by a program but never freed. This leads to excessive memory consumption and eventually leads to a system crash. 
- Wild Pointers: A pointer that never be initialize with valid object or address called wild pointer.
- Dangling Pointers: Assume there is a pointer that refers to memory which was deallocated earlier in the program, that pointer is called a dangling pointer.


## Smart pointers - Types

There are several different types of smart pointers defined in `<memory>`.

- `std::unique_ptr`
- `std::shared_ptr`
- `std::weak_ptr`
- `std::auto_ptr` (replaced by `std::unique_ptr`)

## Smart pointers - unique pointer 2/2

We can not copy a `unique_ptr<>` but we can transfer ownership. 

::: {.columns}
:::: {.column width="33%"}
```{dot}

//| label: move-ownership
//| fig-width: 3
digraph ownership {
  bgcolor="transparent";

      fillcolor="#f5f5f5", color=black];
  p2 [label="P2", shape=box, style=filled,
      fillcolor="#d5e8d4", color=black];

  p1 -> obj [color=gray75,
             label=<<FONT COLOR="red" POINT-SIZE="20">&#10008;</FONT>>];
  p2 -> obj [color=black, penwidth=1.5];

  { rank=same; obj; }
}
```
We can only transfer the control of object to P2

## Smart pointers - shared pointer

By using `shared_ptr`, more than one pointer can point to same object at a time, and it will maintain a reference counter using the `use_count()` method.

::: {.columns}
:::: {.column width="33%"}
```{dot}
//| echo: false
//| label: move-ownership
//| fig-width: 3
digraph ownership {
  bgcolor="transparent";
  rankdir=BT;
  node [fontname="Helvetica-Bold"];

  obj [label="Object", shape=circle, style=filled,
       fillcolor="#d5e8d4", color="#d5e8d4", fontsize=18];

  p1 [label="P1", shape=box, style=filled,
      fillcolor="#f5f5f5", color=black];
  p2 [label="P2", shape=box, style=filled,
      fillcolor="#d5e8d4", color=black];

  p1 -> obj [color=black, penwidth=1.5];
  p2 -> obj [color=black, penwidth=1.5];

  { rank=same; obj; }
}
```
We can maintain the reference count, in this case $2$.

## Smart pointers - weak pointer

A `weak_ptr` is a smart pointer that holds a non-owning reference to an object, i.e a `shared_ptr` without a reference counter. 
The reason is to avoid the circular dependency created by two or more object pointing to each other using `shared_ptr`.


::: {.columns}
:::: {.column width="33%"}
```{dot}
//| echo: false
//| label: move-ownership
//| fig-width: 3
digraph ownership {
  bgcolor="transparent";
  rankdir=BT;
  node [fontname="Helvetica-Bold"];

  obj [label="Object", shape=circle, style=filled,
       fillcolor="#d5e8d4", color="#d5e8d4", fontsize=18];

  p1 [label="P1", shape=box, style=filled,
      fillcolor="#f5f5f5", color=black];
  p2 [label="P2", shape=box, style="filled,dashed",
      fillcolor="#eaf3ea", color=gray40];

  p1 -> obj [color=black, penwidth=1.5];
  p2 -> obj [color=gray40, style=dashed];

  { rank=same; obj; }
}
```
Here `object` is still owned by `P1` and `P2` is a none owing reference.
